beats: Hook: reversible circuits on three bits can express only 40,320 (8!) of the 16,777,216 (8^8) possible 3-bit functions; give them one spare bit and the reversible count jumps to 16! = 20,922,789,888,000, about 21 trillion. Why does one bit buy so much? (line_qc_revers_hat_pegs: a reversible function hangs every hat on its own peg, any function may pile several on one; line_qc_revers_second_rack: one more bit doubles the pegs and the list of arrangements runs off across the floor.) Cast for QC07-01 to QC07-04 (her lecture Q25-08 and the Q24-13 parts): the keeper (short, round, older; bowl haircut, round spectacles, knee-length work coat), who never throws anything away, and the rookie (young; two bunches, dungarees, big sneakers), who would; the cast is set by line_qc_revers_fresh_card, so make it first.

Her three questions (Q25-08 02:50-05:16): can a quantum computer do what a classical one does (expressiveness), how cheaply (efficiency), and what insight makes quantum algorithms faster; lettered on paper, no drawing (or reuse line_course_map).

NAND alone builds every classical circuit (07:06-09:53): line_qc_revers_one_brick_town. But it is not reversible: two inputs, one output, and an output of 1 could come from three different inputs (reuse line_qc_undo_and_bulb from QC05-01).

The fix: a Toffoli gate with its target set to 1 computes NAND and keeps both inputs (10:06-12:34): the keeper never erases; he writes each answer on a fresh card and leaves the inputs as they were (line_qc_revers_fresh_card); reuse line_qc_build_two_keys (QC05-06: the chest that opens only when both keys turn).

Toffoli is universal for classical circuits, not for quantum ones (12:34-13:39); its price is 2 H + 7 T + 6 CNOT, and Clifford + T is universal (13:53-14:19; Nielsen & Chuang fig. 4.9: check in FACTS.md; reuse line_qc_build_lock_inside).
Spare qubits: one in theory, up to one per NAND in practice (15:12-18:48): the fresh stack runs low and the kept cards pile up (line_qc_revers_card_haul); this pile is the garbage of QC07-02.

The counting argument (18:55-30:09; tape Q24-13.notes p1-p2): reversible functions on n bits are the shuffles of 2^n items, (2^n)!, against (2^n)^(2^n) functions in all; with one extra bit the shuffles already outnumber all the 3-bit functions (back to line_qc_revers_hat_pegs and line_qc_revers_second_rack; code letters 8!, 8^8 and 16!). Honest note on screen: counting shows there is room, not how to build it; Bennett 1973 gives a construction, with more spare bits.
Clip Q25-08 30:12-30:43: "reversibility will hurt the expressiveness, but not a lot".
In practice: a special accelerator, like GPUs (clip 32:38 up to 33:05 only: the stock-market remark at 33:05-33:32 is never used; reuse line_gpu).

Honest limits (Q24-13): a quadratic speed-up does not survive the error-correction overhead unless the problem is huge (clip 15:06-15:59; Babbush et al., PRX Quantum 2021: check in FACTS.md): firing up a giant wood oven for one slice of toast (line_qc_revers_oven_toast) pays only when you bake for a banquet (line_qc_revers_oven_banquet), which is why exponential speed-ups are the targets. For machine learning on classical data the speed-up is still in doubt (clip 16:56-17:22; caption only, no drawing).

Cover (line_qc_cover_07_01; for the X post and thumbnails, not a film beat): the rookie sweats at a giant wood oven holding one slice of bread on a long peel; the keeper munches toast from a little toaster.
